items.prompt: The importer has a 2 MB file bound AND a 100,000-character bound on the notes field. Why isn't the file bound alone enough?
items.answer: They guard different costs: the file bound limits parsing, the field bound limits one stored record
distractors: The file bound is advisory in the browser; the per-field bounds are the ones that get enforced
JSON escaping inflates the byte count, so the 2 MB file bound is measured unreliably on its own
The field bound exists to keep ids unique across huge batches, which the file bound does not
items.explanation: Two different resources are being protected: parse-time work (bounded before JSON.parse even runs) versus long-term storage and render cost per record. One record with a 1.9 MB notes field passes the file bound comfortably.

items.prompt: A notes field holds exactly 100,000 characters. Accepted or rejected?
items.answer: Accepted - the check is a strict greater-than, so the limit is inclusive
distractors: Rejected - the check uses greater-than-or-equal, an off-by-one trap
Accepted, but the notes are silently truncated to 99,999 characters
Rejected, because the 2 MB file bound trips first on a field that size
items.explanation: item.length > 100000 fails only at 100,001. Probing the exact boundary is the cheap test that documents whether a limit is inclusive - 100,000 characters is well under 2 MB, so the file bound stays out of it.

items.prompt: Record 2 has BOTH an oversized role field and an unknown status. Which error message does the user see?
items.answer: 'Application 2: role must be bounded text.' - the field loop runs first
distractors: 'Application 2: unknown status.' - domain rules outrank the type checks
Both problems are reported together in one combined error message
'Application 2: expected an object.' - the generic guard fires first
items.explanation: All nine fields pass through the type-and-bound loop before id, company, status, date or URL rules run; the validator stops at the first failure it meets in program order.

items.prompt: The date 2026-02-30 matches the YYYY-MM-DD regex and new Date('2026-02-30T00:00:00Z') does not throw. What finally rejects it?
items.answer: The round trip: toISOString() yields March 1, which no longer equals the input
distractors: Number.isFinite, because a rollover date produces a NaN timestamp
The regex, which already encodes how many days each calendar month may legally have
No check does - the impossible date is accepted and stored exactly as typed
items.explanation: JavaScript's Date silently converts impossible dates into real ones. A validator that stopped at isNaN would bless 2026-02-30; only re-formatting and comparing exposes the rollover.

items.prompt: A record's url is javascript:alert(1). new URL() parses it successfully and the allowlist branch calls fail('URL must use http or https.'). What does the user actually see?
items.answer: 'URL must be an absolute http or https URL.' - the catch swallows fail()
distractors: 'URL must use http or https.', exactly as the allowlist line specifies
No error at all: javascript: URLs are absolute, so the record is accepted
'The file is not valid JSON.', because the outer catch rethrows everything
items.explanation: fail() throws inside the try, so the catch intercepts the validator's own error and substitutes the generic message. The record is still rejected - the security property holds - but the more specific message is unreachable. A try should wrap only the call that can throw (new URL), never the validation after it.

items.prompt: The specific 'URL must use http or https.' message is unreachable, yet the suite never flagged it. Which testing habit let that slip through?
items.answer: The rejection tests use a bare rejects.toThrow(), so any error message passes
distractors: The URL cases were missing entirely from the parameterized payload list
The tests mocked new URL, so the real parser never actually executed
Vitest cannot compare thrown error messages across async promise boundaries at all
items.explanation: Rejected-for-any-reason is a much weaker claim than rejected-for-this-reason. A message-level assertion would have caught the swallowed branch; pinning exact messages is what makes a test notice when the wrong guard fires.

items.prompt: A 600-record backup has one malformed record somewhere in the middle. What ends up in storage after the import attempt?
items.answer: Nothing changes: the whole array is validated before storage.set runs
distractors: The 599 valid records are saved and the malformed one is skipped
Records before the bad one are saved; the records after it are lost
The old data is cleared first, so the user is left with an empty list
items.explanation: parseJobBackup validates the whole array and throws before commitJobBackup ever calls storage.set. Validation completes before persistence, so invalid row 500 cannot leave the first 499 rows saved - the tests pin storage.set at zero calls for every rejection.

items.prompt: There is no database and no transaction API here. What makes the import's write atomic anyway?
items.answer: The replacement is a single storage.set of one serialized array under one key
distractors: The await in commitJobBackup makes the whole write sequence atomic
A try block around the write rolls back the partial writes when one fails
Each record is written separately, but inside one queued microtask batch
items.explanation: Atomicity must come from an operation that actually provides it; await and try blocks provide neither. One storage.set of one value either happens or does not - the storage operation's own contract is the transaction boundary.

items.prompt: exportJobBackup serializes the applications and then immediately runs its own output through parseJobBackup. What is that guarding against?
items.answer: Producing a backup that its own importer would refuse to restore
distractors: Slow exports: a parse pass first warms the JSON engine's caches
Concurrent edits mutating the applications array mid-serialization
The 2 MB bound: an export above the limit is truncated to fit it
items.explanation: The code comment says it directly: never generate a backup the importer cannot restore. If app state somehow violates the schema, export fails loudly instead of producing a poisoned file - the failure moves from restore day to backup day, when the data still exists.

items.prompt: A backup holds a valid Acme record followed by a second record that reuses the same id. What is the outcome?
items.answer: The whole file is rejected ('id is missing or duplicated.'); nothing is stored
distractors: The duplicate is skipped and the remaining records import normally
Both records import, and the UI later de-duplicates them by their id when rendering
The second record overwrites the first one, so the last write wins
items.explanation: An ids Set accumulates across the map; the second occurrence fails with the per-record index in the message. Rejection of the entire batch is the stated policy, not a side effect.

items.prompt: A record omits the location and notes keys entirely. What does the importer do with them?
items.answer: They default to empty strings via ?? before the type-and-bound check
distractors: It fails with 'location must be bounded text.' since location is a required field
The record imports with undefined fields that later render as 'undefined'
The missing keys fail the envelope check before the records are examined
items.explanation: record[field] ?? '' encodes the schema answer to 'which fields can be omitted?' - all of them except what later domain rules demand (id, company, status). Omitted is acceptable, a wrong type is not: notes: 123 is rejected.

items.prompt: A backup holds 10,001 applications. When is it rejected?
items.answer: Right after the envelope check, before any single record is validated
distractors: After all 10,001 records are checked, so the message names the bad one
It is accepted: the cap applies to serialized bytes, not to the record count
At write time, when the storage host refuses the oversized stored value
items.explanation: The cap bounds the validator's own work. The regression test is named for exactly this: rejects more than 10,000 applications WITHOUT validating each one. At exactly 10,000 the batch is accepted - the limit is inclusive, like the field bounds.

items.front: Daybook's import validates the entire payload, then performs exactly one storage.set of the serialized array (src/jobBackup.js:4-7, 60-64). State the guarantee, and why the {format, version} envelope exists.
items.back: Guarantee: invalid row 500 can never leave the first 499 saved, and a failed parse or rejected host write leaves displayed applications unchanged. The envelope distinguishes job backups from calendar data and gives future migrations a version number to branch on.

items.front: The URL allowlist calls fail() INSIDE the try whose catch produces the generic 'absolute http or https URL' message (src/jobBackup.js:43-51). Name the bug pattern and the two-part fix.
items.back: The catch swallows the validator's own exception, making the specific message unreachable (records are still rejected, so security holds). Fix: wrap only new URL() in the try and run the allowlist check after it; and assert exact error messages in tests so an unreachable branch cannot stay invisible.

items.front: The date rule is regex + Number.isFinite + a toISOString round-trip equality (src/jobBackup.js:38-42). What does each layer catch that the others miss?
items.back: The regex pins the YYYY-MM-DD shape, finiteness rejects unparseable garbage, and only the round trip catches rollover dates like 2026-02-30 that the Date constructor silently converts to March 1. A NaN-only validator blesses impossible calendar dates.

items.front: Daybook fully validates a backup file the app itself exported (src/jobBackup.js:5-18). Why treat your own export as untrusted input?
items.back: The file left the trust boundary: it can be edited, truncated, produced by another tool or an older version. JSON.parse proves syntax, not meaning - an array of numbers is valid JSON but not an application list. Export even re-parses its own output, so the app can never mint a backup its importer refuses.
